title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
This incident is a training-data sourcing failure at the foundation of two deployed AI music generation systems. The core allegation is that Suno and Udio ingested copyrighted recordings, including content scraped from YouTube, Deezer, and Genius, without licence or permission, and that the resulting models can reproduce identifiable portions of those recordings on demand. The failure is located at the data-collection stage, before any model was trained or product was shipped, meaning no downstream content filter or output review would have addressed it. Demonstrating the problem required only that plaintiffs prompt the systems and compare outputs to known originals, a check that was apparently never done by the companies before deployment.

The outputs themselves are the evidentiary crux. Plaintiffs generated dozens of results resembling specific named recordings, including near-identical versions of well-known songs, by supplying targeted prompts. That is a model reproducing training material as fact-of-output, the generative equivalent of a system asserting a stored string verbatim. A systematic red-team exercise, sampling model outputs against a library of copyrighted works before launch, could in principle have surfaced this, though whether it would have changed the training pipeline is not established.

What is not established is that any court in the United States has issued a final verdict on the central copyright claims, that the companies acted with the intent alleged, or that the settlements reached with some major labels resolve the broader litigation. Lawsuits from independent artists, class actions, a German court ruling for GEMA, and further suits from music publishers remain at various stages, and allegations in those proceedings are not findings.

summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records, have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular AI music generators. The companies are accused of scraping thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models and of directly reproducing sections of famous songs. The record labels submitted a massive list of copyrighted works they claim were used for training, featuring artists like The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Bruce Springsteen, Michael Jackson, and many others. One lawsuit was filed in New York against Udio, while another was filed in Massachusetts against Suno, the company's headquarters location.

The record labels demonstrated their allegations by creating AI-generated songs using specific prompts and comparing the outputs to original copyrighted recordings. They generated 29 different outputs resembling Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode" and created a near-identical version of Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You" using targeted prompts. The labels claim both companies have refused to disclose their training data and argued their practices constitute fair use. The lawsuits also target unnamed individuals accused of helping scrape the music, setting up a major legal battle over generative AI services.
